rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so the critical first question is: what is the performance floor of the simplest possible model? config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA n2000) is the most minimal configuration in the search space—it uses a linear projection, a single profile (no aggregation), and no image or fusion components. Running this first establishes the baseline RNA signal strength with minimal assumptions, which is essential for interpreting all subsequent experiments. If this baseline is already competitive, it tells us that complex encoders (scVI, scGPT) or multimodal fusion may offer diminishing returns; if it is weak, it motivates exploring richer RNA encoders or adding the image modality. Choosing the simplest configuration first also minimizes computational cost, preserving budget for the many follow-up comparisons (encoder choice, profile setting, aggregation, fusion) that will follow. This single experiment reduces the most uncertainty with the least risk of confounding, since no design choice is 'turned on' simultaneously.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485), the dominant uncertainty is whether the image modality carries useful signal at all. config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) provides the cleanest possible comparison to the existing baseline: same profile setting (singleprofile), same simplicity level (no aggregation, no fusion), differing only in modality. If image_only approaches or exceeds 0.485, it confirms image features are informative and justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion. If it falls well below, it suggests RNA is the primary signal source, allowing us to prune all multimodal configs and focus budget on RNA encoder/aggregation choices. This single experiment resolves the largest structural design question (modality value) while keeping the comparison maximally controlled, making it the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA-only, single profile, PCA n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (image-only, ResNet50) is much weaker at 20.8%, confirming RNA is the dominant signal. However, we have only one RNA data point, so we cannot tell whether PCA (a simple linear projection) is near-optimal or whether a learned nonlinear encoder would substantially improve representation quality. Question: config_004 (RNA-only, single profile, scvi_n200) changes only the RNA encoder from PCA to scvi while holding profile setting and all other factors constant, giving a clean A/B comparison of representation quality. Why this is the best next experiment: With only 2 completed runs, the highest-uncertainty design axis is whether the RNA encoder choice matters. If scvi significantly outperforms PCA, it justifies investing remaining budget in learned encoders (scvi, scgpt) and their multiprofile variants; if not, PCA suffices and we should pivot to testing aggregation/multiprofile or fusion strategies. This single experiment maximally reduces uncertainty about the most fundamental representation decision before committing budget to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: scvi_n200 is our best RNA encoder (0.520 acc) vs pca_n2000 (0.485), and image alone (resnet50) is very weak (0.208). The key unresolved question is whether the multiprofile setting with aggregation improves upon the singleprofile baseline. This experiment (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean, single-variable extension of config_004 (same encoder, same modality; only profile setting changes from single to multi with avgpool aggregation). It isolates the effect of multiprofile+aggregation while holding the best-known encoder fixed. Choosing avgpool over transformer keeps the test conservative and interpretable: if avgpool already helps, multiprofile is validated; if it doesn't, we can then test transformer (config_006) to rule out aggregation-method effects. This is the highest-information next step because the multiprofile decision gates many downstream configurations and will determine whether to invest further in aggregation design or pivot to encoder/fusion questions.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieved 0.650 acc, a large jump over config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile, 0.520), confirming multiprofile is highly beneficial. However, we have only tested one aggregation method (avgpool) in the multiprofile setting. Uncertainty: it is unknown whether transformer aggregation captures inter-profile dependencies that simple averaging misses, which could further improve performance or confirm avgpool sufficiency. This experiment (config_006) changes exactly one variable—aggregation from avgpool to transformer—while holding the best-known RNA encoder (scvi_n200) and profile setting (multiprofile) constant. It is the most informative next step because it isolates the aggregation design choice, directly extends our strongest result, and the outcome will inform aggregation selection for all subsequent multimodal experiments, making it the highest-value use of the next budget slot.

Evidence: The multiprofile setting produced a large boost for scvi_n200 (0.520 single → 0.650 multiprofile, ~13 pts), while aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) showed negligible difference. However, we have no multiprofile result for pca_n2000 (only its singleprofile baseline at 0.485). Question: Does the multiprofile advantage generalize across RNA encoders, or is it specific to learned encoders like scvi_n200? config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) directly isolates this by adding multiprofile to the exact encoder from config_001, holding aggregation at the simpler avgpool (justified by the near-identical avgpool/transformer results). This is the best use of the next budget slot because it clarifies whether 'multiprofile' is a universal design lever or an encoder-interaction effect, which will determine whether we should prioritize encoder choice or profile setting in subsequent multimodal experiments.

Evidence: Multiprofile RNA models with scvi_n200 (config_005/006) achieve ~0.65 acc, far outperforming singleprofile and image-only baselines. Aggregation choice (avgpool vs transformer) appears negligible for scvi_n200 (0.650 vs 0.653). However, the scgpt encoder is completely untested, leaving open the question of whether a different RNA representation could further improve performance. Question: config_009 (scgpt, multiprofile, transformer) directly isolates the encoder effect by holding profile setting and aggregation constant relative to config_006, giving a clean scgpt-vs-scvi_n200 comparison in the strongest setting. Why this is the best next experiment: Before committing budget to multimodal fusion experiments (which add complexity and depend on choosing the best RNA encoder), we need to know whether scgpt offers a meaningful improvement over scvi_n200. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200 here, it reshapes the multimodal search; if it underperforms, we can confidently anchor multimodal experiments on scvi_n200. This single-variable test maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The strongest result to date is config_006 (RNA-only, multi-profile, scVI n200, transformer) at 0.653 acc. RNA encoders rank clearly: scVI n200 > PCA n2000 > scGPT. Image-only with ResNet50 is very weak (0.208), but ViT-L has not been tested at all. The central unresolved question is whether the image modality can add value on top of the strong RNA baseline, and whether a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) changes that picture. This experiment (config_038) pairs the proven-best RNA setup (scVI n200, multi-profile, transformer aggregation) with the strongest available image encoder (ViT-L) and the simplest fusion (concat), isolating the question 'does a strong image representation add complementary signal?' If it beats 0.653, image modality is confirmed useful and we can explore fusion strategies; if it does not, we can rule out image as a useful modality and concentrate remaining budget on RNA-side refinements. This is the highest-information single step because it directly tests the largest unexplored design axis (multimodal fusion) while holding all RNA-side choices at their known-optimal values.

Evidence: config_038 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, concat) is our best result at 0.721 acc, substantially above RNA-only best (0.653) and image-only (0.208), confirming that fusion of a strong RNA encoder with a strong image encoder is highly beneficial. However, we have only tested one fusion strategy (concat) in the multimodal setting. Question: config_039 is identical to config_038 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, isolating the effect of fusion strategy on the best-performing configuration. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean single-variable comparison that directly tests whether the interaction between modalities benefits from learned weighting versus simple concatenation. If weighted fusion improves performance, it signals that modality importance is non-uniform and we should prioritize fusion design; if it does not, concat is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward other axes (e.g., aggregation or RNA encoder choice in the multimodal setting). This is the highest-information, lowest-risk next step given the limited budget.

The strongest result so far (config_039, multimodal scVI+ViT-L, multi-profile, transformer, weighted: 0.725) shows a ~7-point gain over the best RNA-only model (config_006: 0.653), but we have almost no information about the image modality's standalone contribution with ViT-L. The only image experiment (config_010, ResNet50 single-profile) was very weak (0.208) and used a different encoder. Config_015 (image-only, multi-profile, ViT-L, transformer) uses the same image encoder, profile setting, and aggregation as the best multimodal model, cleanly isolating the image modality's contribution. If image-alone performance is high (~0.60+), the multimodal gain is largely additive and future effort should focus on image-side improvements; if it is low (~0.30-0.40), the gain reflects true cross-modal synergy and we should prioritize fusion-strategy exploration. This single experiment resolves the largest remaining uncertainty about where the performance is coming from, directly guiding all subsequent design decisions under the limited budget.
